findings.claim: "They are not concentrated at the weakest anomalies: 46% of all misses have an anomaly Δχ² > 10^4 (median 6,900), and at smaller separations the model recovers 0.884 of the weakest detectable anomalies (Δχ² < 500)."
findings.evidence: I recomputed this with my own code (scratch verify5/results/recompute.py, recompute2.py) on the final-test rows (360,472 rows; 42,805 detectable anomalies, all with weight 1; 2,207 argmax misses). The data contradict the claim in the relative sense, and the numbers quoted as evidence hide this. (1) 63.9% of detectable anomalies have Δχ² > 1e4 and their median is 34,037. For the misses it is 46.1% and 6,932, so the misses sit at weaker anomalies than the population. (2) Δχ² < 500 holds 6.9% of detectable anomalies but 17.1% of misses; Δχ² < 2000 holds 18.9% against 35.1%. Argmax miss rate by bin: 12.8% (160-500), 7.7% (500-2k), 5.6% (2k-1e4), 5.1% (1e4-1e5), 2.8% (>1e5). (3) At smaller separations (s < 2.92; 38,071 detectable, 993 misses) the concentration is strong. Δχ² < 500 is 7.1% of the events but 31.4% of the misses (miss rate 11.6%, against 2.6% overall and 0.4% above 1e5). Δχ² < 2000 is 19.1% of the events and 56.5% of the misses. So 0.884 is the lowest recall of any Δχ² bin at those separations (0.974 overall), not evidence against concentration. (4) The paper contradicts itself: Fig. params (recall 0.904 -> 0.972 with Δχ²), its caption ("the lower recall at ... weak injected evidence", l.759) and l.749-750 ("recall is lower toward ... weak injected anomalies"). (5) The completeness critic's own recommended fix was to name two sources of misses, near-floor anomalies at s<3 and wide separations. The rewrite names one and denies the other. (6) The only guard is miss_dchi2_gt_1e4_pct > 30. With figures_stats set to 31, make_macros.py in a scratch copy exits 0, although 31% would be half the population share. recall_weakest_not_wide is unguarded: set to 0.5, the build still passes.
findings.fix: Replace the sentence with the two-source account. Wide binaries (s > 2.9: 11% of detectable anomalies, 55% of misses) are missed about a quarter of the time at every evidence strength. At smaller separations the misses are near-floor anomalies (Δχ² < 2000: 19% of those detectable anomalies, 57% of their misses; recall 0.884 at Δχ² < 500 against 0.974). Derive the share-of-misses vs share-of-population numbers in make_figures.py. Replace the guard with one that compares them, e.g. require the not-wide miss share at Δχ²<2000 to exceed the population share, or drop 'not concentrated' entirely.
findings.verdict_note: Reproduced with my own code on the final-test rows at HEAD 9e95776 (scratch verify5/adv_results_b/a01.py; all 42,805 detectable anomalies have weight 1; 2,207 argmax misses). Detectable anomalies: 63.9% have Δχ²>1e4, median 34,037. Misses: 46.1%, median 6,932. Δχ²<500 is 6.9% of events but 17.1% of misses. Δχ²<2000 is 18.9% of events but 35.1% of misses. Miss rate by bin: 12.8/7.7/5.6/5.1/2.8%. At s<2.92 (38,072 events, 993 misses): Δχ²<500 is 7.1% of events but 31.4% of misses (recall 0.884). Δχ²<2000 is 19.1% of events but 56.5% of misses. Recall climbs 0.884/0.945/0.970/0.982/0.996 across the bins. So 0.884 is the lowest-recall bin at small separations, and at those separations the misses are concentrated at weak anomalies. Fig. params (metrics.json: 0.904→0.972) and l.749-750 say recall is lower toward weak anomalies. The round-4 critic (gaps[0]) asked the paper to name near-floor anomalies at s<3 as a second source; the rewrite denies it. Guards: in a git-archive copy, miss_dchi2_gt_1e4_pct=31 exits 0 and 29 fires, so the guard can fire, just at a loose bound. recall_weakest_not_wide=0.5 exits 0 (unguarded). Read as absolute share of all misses, 'not concentrated' is literally true (only 17% are below 500). But the evidence offered is misleading and it contradicts the small-separation subset the sentence itself cites. Major is defensible. Minor nit: 38,072, not 38,071.

findings.claim: "It falls to 0.51 in a low-support corner at log q < -5, and it is also lower, 0.69--0.96, in the well-populated column of widest separations at stellar mass ratios (s > 2.9, q > 10^-2)"
findings.evidence: Recomputed plane (recompute2.py, identical to make_figures): wide-column cells at q>=1e-2 are 0.962 (log q -2..-1.5, Nd 210), 0.933 (-1.5..-1, Nd 434), 0.715 (-1..-0.5, Nd 1298), 0.690 (-0.5..0, Nd 2595); plane median 0.974. The upper end 0.962 is 0.012 below the median, within one binomial SE (sqrt(.962*.038/210)=0.013), and above its own row neighbour at log s bin 1 (0.959), so 'lower' is not supported for it. The weakness is confined to q > 0.1: wide & q>=0.1 argmax recall 0.698 (n=3,893) against 0.943 for wide & 0.01<=q<0.1 (n=644); 96.7% of wide misses have q >= 0.1. The minimum cell (0.514) is at log s -0.23..0 (s 0.58-1.0), the middle of the separation axis, not a corner.
findings.fix: Say it falls to 0.69-0.72 in the two best-populated widest-separation cells at q > 0.1 (Nd 1,298 and 2,595), and compute the range over q >= 0.1 in make_figures.py. Call the minimum 'the lowest populated mass-ratio row' rather than a corner, and guard as in results-02.
findings.verdict_note: The numbers reproduce (a03.py). Wide-column cells at q≥1e-2 are 0.962 (Nd 210), 0.933 (434), 0.715 (1298) and 0.690 (2595); the plane median is 0.974. The 0.962 cell sits 0.012 below the median, about 1 binomial SE (0.013), and above its own row's s-bin-1 cell (0.959). So the range's upper end is not meaningfully 'lower', and the text overstates how far the weakness extends. Wide q≥0.1 recall is 0.698 (n=3,893) against 0.943 for 0.01≤q<0.1 (n=644), and 96.7% of wide misses have q≥0.1. The 0.933 cell is also genuinely lower (about 3.4 SE). The 'corner' objection does not hold. The min cell (0.514, Nd 35) is at log q -5.5..-5, s 0.58-1.0. Those are the only two populated cells of the lowest populated q row, i.e. the bottom tip of the populated region, so 'low-support corner' is a fair description of the figure as drawn. Keep the range fix (0.69-0.72 at q>0.1, or compute over q≥0.1). Drop the corner rewording.

findings.claim: "Across the evaluation pool, 39.5% of events ... Of the events generated as binary or planetary lenses, only 37.3% show a detectable anomaly and keep the anomalous label; 54.6% ... are labelled as single lenses."
findings.evidence: These percentages are unweighted over stored events. keep_prob is exactly 0.15 for every generated binary labelled PSPL or Flat and 1.0 for everything else (keepprob.py). Weighted by 1/keep_prob, i.e. over the events generated as binaries, only 8.2% show a detectable anomaly and 80.0% are labelled single lenses; overall relabelling is 71.6%. The text says 'of the events generated as binary or planetary lenses' and does not mention the subsampling here, which is described only at l.536. It thus conflicts with Fig. plane's left panel, which the caption defines as 'of generated binaries, the weighted fraction whose anomaly clears the detectability floor' (overall 8.2%).
findings.fix: Say 'of the stored (subsampled) events', or quote the weighted fractions (8.2% / 80.0%) with a pointer to the subsampling in Sec. eval.
findings.verdict_note: The numbers reproduce (a07.py). keep_prob is 0.15 for every generated binary labelled PSPL or Flat and 1.0 otherwise. Weighted over generated binaries: 8.2% detectable, 80.0% single lens, 71.6% overall relabelled (pool; test 8.2/79.9/71.6). The unweighted 37.3/54.6/39.5 are shares of stored events. But the paragraph explicitly scopes itself to the stored data ('Across the evaluation pool'), and its conclusion is about training examples ('asks the network ... on about a third of its examples'), where unweighted shares are the right quantity. The weighted figures would make its point stronger, not weaker. Fig. plane's caption explicitly says 'weighted', so 'conflicts with Fig. plane' is overstated. What remains is a missing pointer to the subsampling at l.263: readers may take 37.3% as the generator's detectability fraction. Minor clarity fix, not a wrong number.

findings.claim: cmd("bmlEffMinLogq", f"{fs['eff_cond_recall_min_logq_hi']:.0f}") prints the upper log q edge of the minimum cell in 'log q < \bmlEffMinLogq'
findings.evidence: The q grid has half-integer edges (-6, -5.5, ..., 0), and '.0f' rounds half to even: format(-5.5,'.0f') = '-6', format(-3.5,'.0f') = '-4', format(-4.5,'.0f') = '-4'. The current edge is -5.0, so the rendered '-5' is correct. If the minimum moved to a cell whose upper edge is -5.5 or -3.5, the sentence would print a bound the cell violates, e.g. 'log q < -6' for a cell spanning [-6, -5.5). No guard would catch it.
findings.fix: Format with '.1f' (or '%g'), or assert the edge is an integer before formatting.
findings.verdict_note: Confirmed in my scratch copy. Setting eff_cond_recall_min_logq_hi=-5.5 renders \bmlEffMinLogq as '-6', and -3.5 renders '-4'. Python's '.0f' rounds half to even, and make_figures.py stores the half-integer q edges (qe = linspace(-6,0,13)). Either value would print a bound that the cell itself violates ('log q < -6' for a [-6,-5.5) cell), and make_macros exits 0. The bug is latent: the current edge is -5.0, which renders '-5' correctly (min cell log q [-5.5,-5), recomputed), and the hashed artifact is frozen. Minor, with no effect on the current paper.

findings.claim: "On the complete season this sample flags slightly fewer single lenses than all scored ones (\bmlCgSingleFullWindow% = 4.8% against \bmlGullsFaCombined% = 6.3%), so the burden and purity figures here are slightly optimistic." Guard: need(bu["full_window_flag_frac"] < FA_REC_FROZEN). REVISION row 10 and disposition cascade-5 repeat '4.8% vs 6.3% ... (guarded)'.
findings.evidence: The two numbers come from different protocols. 4.8% is the scan's last cut, which is F146 only (144/3000). 6.3% is fa(REC) from transfer_tradeoff_all.json, i.e. the three-band full scoring (2085/33353 = 6.25%). My script (scratchpad/verify5/cascade/fa_sample.py) uses rows_full_fspl5s_seasons_g08{,_f146only}.json from the curve cache. F146 only, like for like: the same 3,000 events give 4.80% (144, which matches the scan's last cut event for event), against 5.75% for all 33,353 scored single lenses (1918). That 5.75% is committed as validation/gulls/transfer_full_fspl5s_seasons_g08_f146only.json by_class 1S1L frac_over_threshold 0.0575. Sample vs the other 30,353: 4.80% vs 5.84%, z=2.34, p=0.019. Three bands, like for like: the scan's three-band last cut gives 5.83% (175), against 6.25% for all (p=0.32 vs the rest). The fourth verifier's cascade-5 evidence had already given the like-for-like 4.80% vs 5.84%. The fix swapped in the three-band population value. The guard cannot test the claim. I set full_window_flag_frac to 0.0575 in a scratch copy, i.e. the sample exactly as representative as the population, like for like. make_gulls_macros.py then ran without error (scratchpad/verify5/cascade/guard_test.py, case 'full-window = all-scored F146 rate'), and the text would still say 'slightly optimistic'. findings.fix: Compare like with like. Either quote 4.8% against the F146-only rate over all scored single lenses (5.75%; add a macro from transfer_full_fspl5s_seasons_g08_f146only.json and put that file in MANIFEST/--list-inputs), or quote the scan's three-band last cut (5.8%) against 6.3%. Change the guard to compare within one protocol, e.g. need(bu_f146['full_window_flag_frac'] < FA_REC_FROZEN_F146), and bound 'slightly' (e.g. ratio > 0.7). Add a fail-closed case where the sample equals the population rate. Correct REVISION row 10 and the cascade-5 disposition text.

It equals the F146-only transfer rows event for event (0 mismatches in 3000). All scored single lenses under F146 give 1918/33353 = 5.75%, the committed frac_over_threshold 0.0575 in transfer_full_fspl5s_seasons_g08_f146only.json. 6.3% is 2085/33353, which is three bands (paper.tex l.1151: the full scoring uses all three bands). Sample vs the other 30,353: z = 2.34, p = 0.019. Three bands: 175/3000 = 5.83% vs 6.25%. The guard at make_gulls_macros.py:560 compares the F146 sample with the three-band population. I patched full_window_flag_frac to 0.0575, and also to 0.0625, and ran the generator with --list-inputs (writes nothing): it ran clean. It fires only at 0.063. REVISION.md l.443 and the cascade-5 disposition repeat '4.8% vs 6.3%'. Why 'partly': (a) The second fix option (three-band 5.8% vs 6.3%) is wrong for this paragraph. The burden and purity figures are F146 (6.2%, and 8.9% weighted). In three bands the rate-weighted sample flags MORE than the population (8.96% vs 8.37%, the value of bmlGullsFaWCombined). Only the F146 pair supports 'slightly optimistic' (4.80% vs 5.75% unweighted, 5.82% vs 6.85% weighted). (b) The severity is borderline. findings.claim: After the per-stratum numbers (giant: lag +5.0 vs +4.5 d, detected 80% vs 89%; Neptune: +6.5 vs +4.5 d, 66% vs 73%): "Premature alerts are therefore no more frequent, alerts come later and detection is lower". Disposition cascade-1: 'Fixed'.
findings.evidence: All numbers were recomputed independently and match the macros: my_reduce.py from the 82 scan_v2 files and Planet_q in the pinned meta parquet, inhouse.py from cascade_trace.npz. Significance per stratum (signif.py): the giant lag differs by one half-day grid step, bootstrap 95% CI of the median difference [-0.5, +2.0] d, Mann-Whitney p=0.19. Neptune detection 543/826 vs 35/48 gives Fisher p=0.35 (in-house Wilson interval about 59-84%). Giant detection p=0.035. Neptune lag p=0.05. Premature 2/149 vs 2/138 and 21/826 vs 2/48 give p=1.0 and 0.36. Pooled over the two strata the directions are clear: detection 67.9% vs 84.9% (p=1e-6), lag +6.5 vs +4.5 d (bootstrap [1.0, 2.75], p=2e-4). The fourth verifier's cascade-1 fix asked to 'qualify Alerts come later (... within 0.5 d for giants)', and its verdict note says the giant lag and the Neptune detection differences are not significant. The text does not carry that qualification, the guards (make_gulls_macros.py 542-546) test only point-estimate order, and the disposition says 'Fixed'.
findings.fix: State that the in-house strata are small (138 and 48 events). Say the direction holds with both strata pooled (detection 68% vs 85%, lag +6.5 vs +4.5 d), but the giant-stratum lag (0.5 d, one grid step) and the Neptune-stratum detection differences are within the sampling noise. Update the cascade-1 disposition to say what was and was not done.
findings.verdict_note: The numbers reproduce (strata.py, from the 82 scan_v2 files, the pinned meta Planet_q and cascade_trace.npz). Giant: RMDC26 119/149 detected, 2/149 premature, lag +5.0 d; in-house 123/138, 2/138, +4.5 d. Neptune: RMDC26 543/826, 21/826, +6.5 d; in-house 35/48, 2/48, +4.5 d. Giant detection Fisher p = 0.035, Neptune detection p = 0.35. Giant lag Mann-Whitney p = 0.19 (bootstrap 95% CI of the median difference [-0.5, 2.0] d). Neptune lag p = 0.050. The text and REVISION.md ('in each stratum') lack the qualification the cascade-1 fix asked for. The guards (make_gulls_macros.py 542-546) test point order only, and the disposition says 'Fixed'. So the defect exists. The proposed fix is wrong, though. Pooling the two strata brings back the mass-ratio composition confound the fourth verification removed: the pooled RMDC26 set is 85% Neptunes (826/975), the in-house set 26% (48/186). So '68% vs 85%, p = 1e-6' and the pooled lag overstate the evidence. Stratified tests (cmh2.py, lagstrat.py): Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel for detection, odds ratio 0.59, p = 0.034; a stratified (van Elteren-type) permutation test for lag, p = 0.027. With three bands: detection p = 0.015, lag p = 2e-4. The joint direction is supported, but only modestly. The text should cite a stratified combination, not pooled rates.

findings.claim: REVISION row 10: "Premature alerts stay rare and no more frequent than in-house". Paper: "Premature alerts are therefore no more frequent", followed by three-band stratum numbers with no direction stated.
findings.evidence: 'No more frequent' holds only for F146 and stratum by stratum (1.3% vs 1.4%, 2.5% vs 4.2%). With three bands, RMDC26 premature alerts are more frequent in both strata: giant 3/149 = 2.0% vs 1/138 = 0.7%, Neptune 8/826 = 1.0% vs 0/48 = 0.0% (macros bmlCgRmGiantPremThree etc.; recomputed). With the two F146 strata pooled, RMDC26 is also higher: 23/975 = 2.36% vs 4/186 = 2.15%, a Simpson reversal from RMDC26's Neptune-heavy mix. None of these differences is resolved (Fisher p = 0.6-1.0). The in-house giant three-band rate also sits below RMDC26's F146 value, and RMDC26's own giant premature rate rises from 1.3% (F146) to 2.0% (three bands), against 'revealing all three bands lowers premature alerts' overall. The unscoped REVISION wording is contradicted by the three-band strata. The paper's juxtaposition leaves the reader to carry 'no more frequent' over to three bands.
findings.fix: Replace 'no more frequent' with 'about as frequent (within the counting noise: 2 vs 2 and 21 vs 2 events)' and scope it to F146. In the three-band clause, say RMDC26's premature rates are the higher ones there (3 vs 1 and 8 vs 0 events). Scope the REVISION bold sentence the same way.
findings.verdict_note: The three-band stratum counts reproduce: RMDC26 giant 3/149 = 2.0% vs in-house 1/138 = 0.7%, Neptune 8/826 = 1.0% vs 0/48. REVISION.md l.443's bold 'Premature alerts stay rare and no more frequent than in-house' is unscoped and follows directly after those three-band numbers. That part is real and minor. In paper.tex l.1441 the sentence follows only the F146 strata, and there it holds by point estimate in both strata (1.34% vs 1.45%, 2.54% vs 4.17%; stratified CMH odds ratio 0.72, p = 0.83). The three-band clause at l.1449-1452 states no direction. So the paper part is at most a risk that readers carry the claim over. Two evidence items are not contradictions. The pooled 23/975 vs 4/186 'Simpson reversal' is the composition confound that stratifying removes. RMDC26's giant stratum going from 2 to 3 premature events does not conflict with the statement about all eligible events (37 to 18 events, 2.2% to 1.1%). The fix is fine: scope 'no more frequent' to F146, soften it to 'about as frequent' with the counts, and say RMDC26 is higher in the three-band strata (all differences unresolved, Fisher/CMH p = 0.47-1.0).

findings.line: 1734-1737 (Data availability); same claim in Sec. limits at 1044-1047
findings.claim: Data availability: "Regenerated at the current code the data are statistically equivalent, not event-identical: a few labels have changed since the released shards were made, which shifts the random stream after the first change (for two held-out shards, 75% of the events reproduce)". Sec. limits: "At the current code the regenerated shards reproduce 75% ... because a few labels changed after the pool was made".
findings.evidence: The 75% (11,257/15,016) is correct. The cause is not supported, and the evidence points the other way. (1) I compared the fourth verifier's regenerations of held-out shard 90 made with the July-21 generator (ef216e2, the first commit containing run_shard.py) and the July-28 one (e25e4d6) against HEAD's regeneration (referee_local_work/raw_test_f002/shard_00090.h5). Params, m_base and labels are identical for all 7,479 events (script verify5/appendix/cmp_july.py). So the code has not changed any label since July 21. The pool was made on AWS from an uncommitted tarball (aws/ud_gen*.sh: 'aws s3 cp .../sim_v5_code.tgz'), with packages installed by unversioned 'pip3 install numpy scipy h5py VBBinaryLensing'. (2) Of the 9 label differences among matched events, 8 are local PSPL against pool NonPSPL (verify5/appendix/labdiff.py). That is the same direction as the stress natural tier's '2.3% fewer detectable anomalies'. The paper's own appendix (1754-1756), Sec. limits (777-779) and validation/gulls/PROVENANCE.md attribute that deficit to the unpinned cloud environment ('even with the July generator'). (3) The fourth-round verdict on text-regeneration-not-bit-identical already stated that "'labels changed since July' is incorrect" and that pinning the generator commit would not help. The applied fix nevertheless wrote in exactly that cause. A reader who checks out an older commit to get event-identical shards would fail.
findings.fix: In both places replace the cause with the environment: shards regenerated outside the original (unpinned) cloud environment reproduce 75% of the events. The single-lens refit that sets a few labels differs between environments, and each changed label shifts the keep/drop random stream. The generator itself gives the same shards at every commit since July 21. Drop 'at the current code' and 'since the released shards were made / after the pool was made'.
findings.verdict_note: Reproduced. I reran cmp_july.py (copy in verify5/adv_appendix/r2). The July-21 (ef216e2) and July-28 (e25e4d6) regenerations of shard 90 (verify4/adv_text/pool_*_90.npz, seed 20260720) are identical to referee_local_work/raw_test_f002/shard_00090.h5 in params (t_anom excluded), m_base and labels. That raw shard was made at 8a8bd4b. labdiff.py gives 11,241 uniquely matched events with 9 label differences: 8 are local PSPL against pool NonPSPL, 1 the reverse. That is the same direction as the stress deficit, which paper.tex:777-779, 1754-1755 and PROVENANCE.md:51-52 blame on the unpinned fleet environment. f79f073 wrote both causes into the paper: 'labels changed after the pool was made' / 'at the current code' at 1044-1047 and 1734-1736, and environment at 1754-1755. So the paper contradicts itself, and the cause it gives at 1044 and 1734 is the one the fourth verdict had rejected. One caveat: the natural pool predates ef216e2 (committed 05:17 on 21 July; base training started 00:03), so a code change in that window cannot be excluded. Even then, 'at the current code' / 'since the released shards were made' would still be wrong. Major is defensible because this is the reproducibility paragraph. The fix is right.

findings.claim: The referee round's per-event inputs are archived in validation/referee_round_archive/, and 'Re-deriving a reported statistic from these requires only the reduction scripts, with two exceptions'. The runner docstring adds: 'so the JSON can be re-reduced without this machine's work directory'.
findings.evidence: The archive is now committed, and all 22 blobs at 9e95776 match referee_round.json's sha256 (git show + hashlib). But its npz files hold only score_nonpspl/logits/label/true_class/keep_prob/test_idx, the stream label/keep_prob/true_class/t_anom arrays and the probability traces. They hold no event parameters or m_base. _threshold_selection_overlap, _floor_overlap and _same_events read WORK/raw_*/shard_*.h5 params. So four statistics quoted in Sec. limits cannot be re-derived from the archive: 75% (bmlRefMatchPct), 19% (bmlRefValPctMatched), and the floor arms' 22%/5% overlap (bmlRefFloorShareLo/Hi). The same holds for 'the events are identical'. Only the 25 label changes re-derive, and they do (25 from the archived label arrays). So the docstring's promise has no implementation.
findings.fix: Add the regenerated shards' params and m_base (or the per-event match flags) to the archive, and add a --from-archive reduction path. Otherwise, list the overlap statistics as a third exception in Data availability and correct the runner docstring.
findings.verdict_note: The core points hold. All 22 archive files match referee_round.json's sha256. The npz files hold no params or m_base. _same_events, _floor_overlap and _threshold_selection_overlap read WORK/raw_*. No committed code reads validation/referee_round_archive/ (grep finds only the test). _archive renames stream_scan_* to stream_scan_all_*, so the docstring's 're-reduced without this machine's work directory' has no implementation. The 25 label changes do re-derive from the archive. However, 'four statistics cannot be re-derived from the archive' is overstated. Matching the archived shipped-model logits against the distributed paper/results/logits.npy (within 1e-3) gives all four (verify5/adv_appendix/r2/logit_match2.py). It finds 11,247/15,016 = 74.9% matched (macro 75), and 19.4% of those are threshold-selection rows (19). Against f002, 3,243 (21.6%) events are shared with f001 (22) and 682 (4.5%) with f005 (5). So all four round to the quoted values. Only the exact counts (11,257; 3,245) and the colour arm's 'identical params' need the raw shards. The defect is really the missing reduction path and the parameter-based definitions, not missing information. Minor is right. Better fix: add a --from-archive reducer, or archive params and m_base. A 'third exception' is only needed if neither is done.

findings.claim: "The logged training epochs processed 376–656 events per second, including data loading and augmentation; the 6 stages took about 22 hours of wall-clock in total."

findings.verdict_note: Recomputed from v5runs/*.log (training split / logged epoch time). The range is 376.3-656.4 ev/s only once stage 6 epoch 3 (21,366 s, 71.4 ev/s) is dropped. findings.claim: "Every stage used AdamW ... and cross-entropy loss with the selection weights of §eval ... (an additional factor 2 on the anomaly class)".
findings.evidence: Sec. eval defines the selection weight as 1/keep_prob only (paper.tex:535-540). The stages' loss weight (ef216e2 train_v5.py compute_weights, unchanged in pipeline/train.py) is 1/keep_prob times a class-balancing factor target/n_eff. That factor gives every class equal keep_prob-corrected total weight, and alpha multiplies the NonPSPL target. This is a class-balanced loss, not a population-weighted one. Someone who follows the rewritten recipe would train with Flat and PSPL (about 61% of events) dominating. The word 'additional' presupposes the class balancing but the recipe never states it.
findings.fix: Write 'cross-entropy loss with class-balanced weights (each class's selection-weighted mass equalised, docs/training.md) and an additional factor 2 on the anomaly class'.
findings.verdict_note: compute_weights (ef216e2 train_v5.py:189-202, used at 318-319; identical in pipeline/train.py:531-544) returns 1/keep_prob times target/n_eff. That equalises each class's keep_prob-corrected mass, with alpha on the NonPSPL target. Sec. eval (paper.tex:535-540) defines the weight only as undoing the by-product subsampling. paper.tex:1762-1764 says 'cross-entropy loss with the selection weights of Sec. eval ... an additional factor 2', which omits the class balancing. docs/training.md:56-60 does state it. This wording predates the round (it is also at 9c04593:1715 and c4bf5f3) but survives the rewrite. Minor. The fix is right.

findings.evidence: Script scratchpad/verify5/stress/faint_mix.py, released model on eval_released_{natural,oor_flat_faint}, weights 1/clip(keep_prob,1e-3,1). Natural precision is 0.726 and the faint tier's 0.026. (a) Faint-tier events reweighted by generator class to the natural class mix (Flat .047, PSPL .063, NonPSPL .676, Per .055, LPV .111, Erupt .047) give prevalence 3.30%, FPR 14.0% and precision 0.152. (b) Natural-tier events reweighted to the faint tier's class mix (Flat .513, PSPL .036, NonPSPL .040, Per .121, LPV .149, Erupt .142) give precision 0.637. So the mix alone, at natural photometry, lowers precision only from 0.726 to 0.637, while faint photometry at the natural mix lowers it to 0.152. The 3.34 log-precision gap splits 0.13 (mix) + 3.21 (faintness) in one order and 1.78 + 1.57 in the other; averaged over the two orders the mix accounts for about 29% and faintness about 71%. The mechanism is that faint photometry makes non-lensing sources raise false anomalies (argmax NonPSPL, faint vs natural): Flat 2.7% vs 0.00%, PeriodicVar 3.8% vs 0.00%, LPV 4.1% vs 0.00%, Eruptive 11.1% vs 0.08%. The Flat-heavy mix then multiplies these. The 0.440 is a prior shift that keeps the tier's FPR of 5.4%, which the Flat-heavy mix dilutes; at the natural class mix the FPR is 14%. The guard `_need(_mix > _det > 1)` compares prevalence factors (17.1x vs 1.66x) and cannot test a statement about precision. The test perturbation ('set mostly by its class mix') only exercises that prevalence guard. Also, 'mix-independent' (CHANGELOG, addendum) is loose: demoted binaries are 91% of the weighted PSPL labels in the natural tier and 52% in the faint tier. At the natural composition the faint microlensing false-anomaly rate would be about 23%, not 26%.
findings.fix: Drop 'set mostly by the sweep's class mix' and the 0.440 prior shift. Say instead that the faint tier's precision reflects faint-photometry false anomalies among flat and variable sources, multiplied by the sweep's flat-heavy mix: at the natural class mix the same faint photometry gives about 0.15 (natural 0.73), and the mix alone at natural photometry would give about 0.64. Record the two reweighted precisions in stress_rescore_local.json and guard them (for example, reweighted-to-natural-mix precision < 0.5 × natural precision). Mirror the change in the model card, evaluation.md, REVISION row 23, CHANGELOG and the stress-03 disposition, and drop 'mix-independent'.

findings.claim: 'Each tier's shards, caches and evaluations are stamped with the code state that made them (WORK/stamp_<tier>.txt, written when the tier's first shard is generated) and reused when present.'
findings.evidence:
How stamp() behaves:
- It writes only if the file is absent, and main() also calls it for every tier. A tier whose shards or evals already exist without a stamp is therefore stamped with the current commit.
- A re-evaluation, or a partial regeneration after a code change, keeps the old stamp.
- The stamp is written before generation, so a failed run leaves a stamp for incomplete shards.

What happened in this run:
- Four reused tiers (natural, planetary, oor_flat_faint, oor_pspl_shortte_current) have stamp files written at 11:13:42, 7 s before 6865de1 was committed (11:13:49), for shards made at 01:47-01:55. They were back-filled by hand, not by the mechanism. Their value, 6016bc6, is correct: shard and eval mtimes (01:47-02:15) fall between 6016bc6 (01:18) and aa68c99 (02:17).
- The widesep, longp and shortte stamps (11:13:55-11:14:13) were written by the script, which matches.
- The corrected tier's cache is the old tier renamed (files named oor_pspl_shortte_0000x.h5). The raw shards of four tiers are 0-byte placeholders, so the reuse path cannot rebuild them.
findings.fix: Record the code inside each shard, cache and eval directory when it is created, and fail when a reused one lacks a stamp. Keep generation and scoring stamps separate. Note in PROVENANCE that four stamps were back-filled.
findings.verdict_note:
Confirmed in the code and on disk.
Code:
- stress_rescore_local.py:82-87: stamp() writes only if the file is absent.
- main() at line 199 calls stamp(t, code) for every tier, so an unstamped tier that already has shards or evals gets the current commit.
- gen() stamps before run_shard, so a failed generation leaves a stamp.
On disk:
- stamp_{natural,planetary,oor_flat_faint,oor_pspl_shortte_current}.txt are dated 11:13:42 and contain g6016bc6. 6865de1 was committed at 11:13:49, and HEAD at 11:13:42 was 943b171, so these were not written by the mechanism.
- The widesep, longp and shortte stamps (11:13:55-11:14:13, g6865de1) precede their shards (11:14:03-11:14:28), consistent with the script writing them.
- The raw shards of the four reused tiers are 0 bytes.
- cache_oor_pspl_shortte_current/ holds oor_pspl_shortte_0000x.h5, whereas memmap() looks for oor_pspl_shortte_current_0000x.h5.
So the reuse path cannot rebuild these tiers, and PROVENANCE's 'regenerate from the seeds' also needs the placeholders deleted. The stamp values themselves are consistent with the mtimes. Minor.

- Detection: in-house 35/48 = 72.9% (Wilson 95% 59-83%) against RMDC26 543/826 = 65.7% (62-69%). The intervals overlap.

findings.claim: "Anomaly precision in this tier falls to 0.026 (64 detectable anomalies), but that number is set mostly by the sweep's class mix ... at the natural prevalence the same rates would give 0.440."
findings.evidence: validation/stress_rescore_local.py:216-222 computes 0.440 as tpr_w*pi/(tpr_w*pi + fpr_w*(1-pi)). It uses the faint tier's aggregate fpr_w of 5.42%, which is diluted by the tier's Flat-heavy negatives. I recomputed from stress_local_work/eval_released_{natural,oor_flat_faint}. Non-anomalous weight in the faint tier is 80% Flat-labelled (per-label false-anomaly rate 3.6%); PSPL-labelled events are at 26.1% and Eruptive at 11.8%. Applying the faint per-label rates to the natural tier's non-anomalous mix (Flat 23%, PSPL 63%, PeriodicVar 4.5%, LPV 4.2%, Eruptive 4.8% by weight) gives FPR 18.0% and precision 0.19 at the natural prevalence of 5.49% (recall 0.734). The paper's 0.440 is not that number. The fourth-round stress-03 finding named exactly this dilution ('the tier's 5.4% false-anomaly rate is diluted by Flat'; natural-mix precision ~0.15). Its disposition says Fixed, but the number was kept. The guard (_mix > _det > 1) checks only the prevalence split, not the rate term. 'Mostly by the mix' still holds in log terms (ln(0.19/0.026)=2.0 vs ln(0.726/0.19)=1.3). However, the quoted counterfactual overstates faint-source precision at natural prevalence 2.3x, which understates the faint failure (natural 0.726).
findings.fix: Replace 0.440 with the natural-mix counterfactual (about 0.19; add it to stress_rescore_local.json by reweighting per-label false-anomaly rates to the natural tier's non-anomalous composition), or drop the sentence. Make the same change in the model card and guard the mix-controlled number.
findings.verdict_note: Reproduced from stress_local_work/eval_released_{natural,oor_flat_faint}. 0.440 is tpr_w*pi/(tpr_w*pi+fpr_w*(1-pi)) with the tier's aggregate fpr_w of 5.42% (stress_rescore_local.py:216-222). findings.claim: "They are not concentrated at the weakest anomalies: 46% of all misses have an anomaly Delta chi^2 > 10^4 (median 6,900), and at smaller separations the model recovers 0.884 of the weakest detectable anomalies (Delta chi^2 < 500)."
findings.evidence: Recomputed from paper/results (final test: 42,805 detectable anomalies, 2,207 argmax misses). Recall rises monotonically with anomaly Delta chi^2: 0.872 (<500), 0.913 (500-1e3), 0.940 (1e3-1e4), 0.949 (1e4-1e5), 0.972 (>1e5). Delta chi^2 < 500 holds 6.9% of detectable anomalies but 17.1% of misses. The median Delta chi^2 of misses is 6,900, against 34,000 for all detectable anomalies; 64% of detectable anomalies exceed 1e4, against 46% of misses. At s < 2.92 the weakest bin holds 7.1% of detectable anomalies but 31% of the misses. The quoted 0.884 is therefore a miss rate of 11.6%, against 2.6% for all s < 2.92 anomalies; it is the second source of misses, not a reassurance. The fourth-round critic #1 asked for near-floor anomalies at s < 3 to be named as that second source, and the rewrite denies it. The guard requires only miss_dchi2_gt_1e4_pct > 30, far below the 64% baseline, so it cannot detect a skew toward weak anomalies. Related, 727-729: the widest stellar-ratio column is called 'also lower, 0.69-0.96', but its cells are 0.962, 0.933, 0.715 and 0.690 against a plane median of 0.974. The deficit sits at q > 0.1, and the guard checks only the minimum.
findings.fix: Say that most misses are wide binaries and that at smaller separations they concentrate at the weakest anomalies (31% at Delta chi^2 < 500, which hold 7% of detectable anomalies; recall 0.884 there against 0.974 overall). Guard the miss distribution against the detectable-anomaly baseline. For the plane, write 0.69-0.72 at q > 0.1.
findings.verdict_note: Recomputed on the final test (42,805 detectable anomalies, 2,207 argmax misses, all weights 1). Recall by anomaly dchi2 bin: 0.872/0.913/0.940/0.949/0.972. The <500 bin holds 6.9% of detectable anomalies and 17.1% of misses. Median dchi2 is 6,932 for misses and 34,037 for all detectable anomalies; 63.9% of detectable anomalies exceed 1e4, against 46.1% of misses. At s<2.92 the weakest bin holds 7.1% of detectable anomalies and 31.4% of misses, with recall 0.884 against 0.974 overall (miss rate 11.6% vs 2.6%). 'Not concentrated at the weakest anomalies' plus 'recovers 0.884' reads as reassurance, although misses are 2.5x (4.4x at s<2.9) over-represented there. This is the second source of misses that fourth-round critic #1 asked to be named. The guard (miss_dchi2_gt_1e4_pct > 30) cannot detect a skew toward weak anomalies. Plane cells in the top-s column at q>=1e-2 are 0.962, 0.933, 0.715 and 0.690, against a median of 0.974. So '0.69-0.96' is a correct range, but the deficit sits at q>0.1. Minor.
